newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major implores voters to ignore Eurosceptics.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major implores voters to ignore Eurosceptics.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday made a personal appeal to British voters to disregard Eurosceptics in his party who have rejected his "wait and see" stance on the European Union's planned single currency.
In a hastily-recorded television address, Major implored voters not to bind his hands when it comes to negotiations over whether to sign Britain up to a single currency.
Major had been on the back foot all day after two junior ministers defied him with campaign statements for the May 1 national election declaring opposition to any plans to scrap Sterling.
The opposition Labour Party, which has a double-digit lead in opinion polls, pounced on Major's failure to sack the two ministers and accused him of feeble leadership.
In the television address, which showed signs of hurried editing, Major appeared to be talking to the rebels within his party as much as he was to the voters.

He made no mention of Labour or its plans on Europe, but stressed that there may be advantages to a single European currency and pledged a referendum before it could be introduced to Britain. He insisted the nation's options must be left open.
"I have not a shred of intention...of surrendering the responsibility for taxation and expenditure to Europe," said Major.
His message was clear: Voters would be choosing him and his policies at the election, not the rebels within his party.

The election statements by junior ministers John Horam and James Paice had reopened wounds that have dogged Major throughout his 6-1/2 years in power and produced one of the most serious threats to his campaign for re-election.
They are among several Conservative candidates have openly appealed to British xenophobia by pledging to oppose a European single currency if they are elected.
At the start of the day, Major was forced to turn his daily news conference into an impassioned plea to his party's Eurosceptics to toe the line.

"Can anybody honestly put their hand on their heart and say that they know for certain what the outcome would be if we were to decide now, precipitately, without the details at this moment, that never in any circumstances were we going to decide to enter a European single currency?" Major said.
Labour leader Tony Blair by contrast, has largely managed to contain differences within his party over policy on Europe and other areas.
Major, Blair said on Wednesday, was incapable of ruling his party or Britain.

"Britain cannot be represented by a government with all the leadership qualities of lemmings. Britain cannot be represented by a government that is fighting among themselves and therefore they cannot fight for Britain," Blair said in Southampton, southern England.

"We are witnessing the collapse of the Conservative Party under the weight of its own divisions. We are seeing the culmination of six years of weak leadership, a prime minister reduced to a laughing stock by his members of parliament, his party now a rabble," Blair added.
